pos: n. (a Benjamite head of a father's house; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chizqi, my strength, from chazaq, to be strong; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:17, and distinct from Hezekiah the king.
biblical_def: Hezeki occurs once, in the Benjamite register: “And Zebadiah, and Meshullam, and Hezeki, and Heber” (1 Chronicles 8:17). The name is the short form of the element that makes up Hezekiah — my strength — but the man is not the king of Judah; he is a Benjamite of Jerusalem, several centuries and one tribe away. The chapter opens with the tribe's head: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1), and a verse near its end tells the reader what the whole list is for: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). That is the key to several chapters of Chronicles. The Chronicler is writing after the captivity for a people re-establishing itself in the land, and he sets down who the heads of the households were and where they lived, because a returned remnant needed to know whose house was whose. A name four words long carried a family's standing in the holy city.

corruption_summary: Similar names are collapsed into one person by careless reading, where Scripture distinguishes tribe, generation and household for each.
corruption_paragraphs: Hezeki and Hezekiah share a root and nearly share a spelling, and the standing temptation — in readers and in reference works alike — is to treat two such names as one man. Scripture guards against it by the detail it gives: this Hezeki is listed among Benjamites in a chapter of Benjamite households at Jerusalem, while Hezekiah was of Judah and of the line of David. A dictionary that merged them would have invented a person; one that notes the difference is doing the reader's work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the purpose of the register: These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:28). The Chronicler wrote for a people putting itself back together, and he told them whose houses stood where. God's dealings run through households, and the record of them is not idle.

pos: n. (father of Amasa, one of the heads of Ephraim who stopped a deportation; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chadlai, commonly explained as resting or forbearing, from chadal, to cease or forbear; named once, 2 Chronicles 28:12.
biblical_def: Hadlai is named once, and the episode he belongs to is one of the most arresting in Chronicles: “Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against them that came from the war” (2 Chronicles 28:12). The northern army had defeated Judah and was bringing home two hundred thousand captives, brethren of their own blood. A prophet met them first: “But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded: and he went out before the host that came to Samaria” (2 Chronicles 28:9), and then these four chiefs took their stand: “And said unto them, Ye shall not bring in the captives hither: for whereas we have offended against the LORD already, ye intend to add more to our sins and to our trespass: for our trespass is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel” (2 Chronicles 28:13). The captives were released and treated with astonishing tenderness: “And the men which were expressed by name rose up, and took the captives, and with the spoil clothed all that were naked among them, and arrayed them, and shod them, and gave them to eat and to drink, and anointed them” (2 Chronicles 28:15).

corruption_summary: The Old Testament is said to lack mercy toward enemies, where 2 Chronicles 28 records the exact deed the Lord Jesus afterwards made a parable of.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim that the Old Testament knows only severity and the New only mercy breaks on this chapter. Four men of the northern kingdom — the apostate kingdom, the one Chronicles has nothing good to say of — stopped their own victorious army, refused to enslave their defeated brethren, clothed the naked from the spoil they had a legal right to keep, fed them, anointed the feeble, set them on asses and carried them home to Jericho. The Lord Jesus told a story in those very terms, of a man who bound up a stranger's wounds and set him on his own beast; and the men in this chapter were Samaritans' ancestors.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ground they gave for the mercy: whereas we have offended against the LORD already, ye intend to add more to our sins (2 Chronicles 28:13). The argument is not sentiment but the fear of God. Men who knew their own guilt would not add to it, and a prophet's word plus four honest chiefs turned an army around.

pos: n. (head of the eighteenth course of the priests; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Happitstsets, with the article, commonly explained as the dispersion or the shattering, from patsats, to break in pieces; named once, 1 Chronicles 24:15.
biblical_def: Aphses heads one of the twenty-four priestly courses: “The seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Aphses” (1 Chronicles 24:15). The chapter sets out the ordering of the priesthood: “Now these are the divisions of the sons of Aaron. The sons of Aaron; Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (1 Chronicles 24:1), and the courses were not assigned by influence: “Thus were they divided by lot, one sort with another; for the governors of the sanctuary, and governors of the house of God, were of the sons of Eleazar, and of the sons of Ithamar” (1 Chronicles 24:5). The purpose is stated plainly: “These were the orderings of them in their service to come into the house of the LORD, according to their manner, under Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him” (1 Chronicles 24:19). This arrangement was still running a thousand years later, and the New Testament opens inside it: “There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia” (Luke 1:5). Abia is the eighth course of this same list. The eighteenth belonged to Aphses, and the system David ordered was the system in which Gabriel found a priest burning incense.

corruption_summary: The priestly courses are called a late invention projected back onto David, where Luke opens his Gospel inside the system and names a course by number.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments date the twenty-four courses to the post-exilic or even Hasmonean period and read 1 Chronicles 24 as a retrojection giving the arrangement David's authority. The New Testament makes an awkward witness for that view, not because it settles the date, but because it shows the list in living operation and treats it as old: Luke dates the annunciation to the days of Herod and places Zacharias “of the course of Abia,” the eighth name in this very chapter, serving his week in order. An administrative list still governing the temple a millennium later is not easily dismissed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's worship is ordered and His order is not arbitrary. Twenty-four courses, assigned by lot so no house could buy precedence, each with its week; and the chapter grounds the whole in what the LORD had commanded Aaron. Aphses had the eighteenth, and his descendants knew which week was theirs.

pos: n. (steward of the house of Elah king of Israel; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Artsa', commonly explained as earthiness, from 'erets, the earth or land; named once, 1 Kings 16:9.
biblical_def: Arza is named once, as the owner of the house in which a king was murdered: “And his servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him, as he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza steward of his house in Tirzah” (1 Kings 16:9). The translators' margin notes that steward renders a Hebrew phrase meaning which was over the house, that is, the chief officer of the royal household. What follows is immediate: “And Zimri went in and smote him, and killed him, in the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his stead” (1 Kings 16:10). Zimri's own reign lasted seven days. The verdict on the house destroyed that night is given a few verses later: “For all the sins of Baasha, and the sins of Elah his son, by which they sinned, and by which they made Israel to sin, in provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their vanities” (1 Kings 16:13). The detail the Holy Ghost chose to record about Elah's last hour is that he was drinking himself drunk, and Scripture had already said why that matters: “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise” (Proverbs 20:1).

corruption_summary: Drunkenness is treated as a private matter or a disease without guilt, where Scripture names it sin, shows its fruit, and excludes the unrepentant drunkard.
corruption_paragraphs: Two accounts of drunkenness compete with Scripture's. One makes it a private liberty that harms no one; the other makes it purely a disease, so that the category of sin does not apply. The Bible is more honest and more hopeful than either. It names drunkenness among the works that shut men out of the kingdom, and it also shows real pity — the drunkard is mocked, deceived, made a fool of, and Proverbs pictures his waking misery with something like compassion. The remedy offered is not management but repentance and the Spirit, and the apostle sets being filled with the Spirit directly against being drunk with wine.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the chapter records without comment: a king of Israel spent his last evening drinking himself drunk in his steward's house, and his captain walked in and killed him. Sin makes a man unguarded. The sentence on the house is given four verses later, and it is for provoking the LORD with vanities.

pos: n. (a conspirator with Pekah against Pekahiah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aryeh, the lion, with the article; named once, 2 Kings 15:25.
biblical_def: Arieh is named once, among the men who killed a king in his own palace: “But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room” (2 Kings 15:25). His name is simply the lion. The king who died was Pekahiah, and the Holy Ghost gives his character in one sentence before recording his end: “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin” (2 Kings 15:24). The assassin's reign is dated in the next notice: “In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned twenty years” (2 Kings 15:27). This is the last age of the northern kingdom, when five of its last six kings came to the throne by murder, and Arieh is one of the men with a sword in that corridor. A man called Lion appears in Scripture for one act, and the act was regicide.

corruption_summary: The collapse of the northern kingdom is explained purely by geopolitics, where Kings gives a theological verdict on every reign and traces the ruin to one founding sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern histories account for Israel's fall by Assyrian expansion, trade routes and dynastic instability, and all of that is true as far as it goes. The book of Kings is doing something else and says so. It assesses every northern reign by one standard — whether the king departed from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin — and that verdict is pronounced on Pekahiah in the verse immediately before his murder. The political instability is reported as the fruit of apostasy, not as its explanation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a nation's politics follow its worship. Jeroboam set up two calves to keep his people from going up to Jerusalem, and two centuries later captains were cutting down kings in the palace at Samaria while an empire gathered on the border. Men called Lion do well in such times, and for a very short while.

pos: n. (a Benjamite head of a father's house; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eder, a flock, or an arrangement; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:15, among the sons of Beriah.
biblical_def: Ader occurs once: “And Zebadiah, and Arad, and Ader” (1 Chronicles 8:15). Three names and nothing else — the verse is as short as a verse gets, and it belongs to the Benjamite register that runs from the tribe's head: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1). Two verses after Ader's, the same list gives Hezeki: “And Zebadiah, and Meshullam, and Hezeki, and Heber” (1 Chronicles 8:17) — a second Zebadiah, in a second household, which is how closely these families are packed. The point of the chapter is given near its end: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Chronicles was written for the returned remnant, and 1 Chronicles 8 is the roll of Benjamin's houses in the holy city. Benjamin had been reduced to six hundred men in the days of the Judges and would give the church the apostle to the Gentiles. Ader is three syllables in the middle of that history.

corruption_summary: A life recorded in one word is counted a life of no significance, where Scripture preserves the names and God promises to forget none of His own.
corruption_paragraphs: A verse of three names is the sort of thing that persuades a reader that most of the Bible is filler, and critical treatments reinforce it by calling such lists archival residue. But a register of this kind answers a question the modern reader does not think to ask: does God keep track of the people nobody writes about? Chronicles says He does, by name, by father's house, by generation, and by the city they lived in. The same Scripture promises a book of life with names in it, and a new name given to him that overcometh.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that obscurity is not oblivion. Ader is one word in one verse of one chapter, and he is in the word of God, which outlasts every monument that ever carried a famous name. The chapter's summary is enough for any believer: heads of the fathers, chief men, and these dwelt in Jerusalem.

pos: n. (a place in Babylonia from which men returned who could not prove their pedigree; also spelt Addon, named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Addan, of uncertain sense, perhaps strong or firm; the translators' margin at Ezra 2:59 reads “or, Addon,” which is the form Nehemiah uses.
biblical_def: Addan is one of the places in Babylonia from which a particular company came up, and the verse that names it records a real difficulty: “And these were they which went up from Telmelah, Telharsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer: but they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel” (Ezra 2:59). The margin at that verse gives Addon as the alternative, and Nehemiah's parallel register uses that form; one place, two spellings, and so one entry here. These men wanted to be counted with Israel and could not prove it, and some of them claimed the priesthood: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). The ruling given was neither a refusal nor an indulgence but a deferral: “And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” (Ezra 2:63). They were to wait for God to answer. It is a hard verse and an honest one.

corruption_summary: The exclusion of the unproven priests is read as cold legalism, where the ruling protected the altar and deliberately left their case open to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2:62 is produced as an example of religion at its most unfeeling: men who had travelled from Babylon to serve were turned away over paperwork. The chapter deserves a closer reading. The priesthood was not a career but an office God had restricted on pain of death, and a man who could not show his line could not be let to the altar without presuming on God. And the ruling given was not a verdict: they were to refrain from the most holy things until a priest should stand up with Urim and with Thummim — that is, until God Himself should answer. The governor would not decide what God had reserved.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sweetness of the New Testament by contrast. No believer in Christ has to produce a pedigree, because our High Priest's line is the only one required and it is proven in the heavens. The men of Addan waited for Urim and Thummim; we are told to draw near with boldness.

pos: n. (a Benjamite son of Shaharaim, born in Moab; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abitub, my father is goodness, from 'ab, a father, and tob, good; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:11, and distinct from Ahitub the priest.
biblical_def: Abitub occurs once: “And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:11). The verse before gives the setting, and it is an unusual note for a genealogy: “And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives” (1 Chronicles 8:8). A Benjamite family in Moab, with a household broken up and wives sent away — the Chronicler records it in passing and leaves the sorrow in it unexplained. The register belongs to the tribe: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1), and its purpose is stated near the end: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Abitub is not Ahitub, the priest of Eli's house and the grandfather of Abiathar; the names differ by a letter and by a tribe, and the dictionary keeps them apart. His name means my father is goodness, which is a notable thing to find in the one Benjamite household Scripture places in exile in Moab.

corruption_summary: Divorce is treated as a private readjustment, where Scripture records its wreckage plainly and the Lord Jesus restored the creation standard.
corruption_paragraphs: The note that Shaharaim begat children in Moab “after he had sent them away” is the kind of clause readers pass over, and modern treatments of marriage would find nothing in it to remark. Scripture is not so casual. The Lord Jesus, pressed on divorce, went back past Moses to the creation ordinance — one man, one woman, one flesh, not to be put asunder — and said that the permission given in the law was granted for the hardness of men's hearts. A sent-away household in a foreign country is exactly what hardness of heart leaves behind.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mercy that runs through a broken record. In the one Benjamite household Scripture locates in Moab, after a putting away, a son is named my father is goodness; and the chapter ends by listing that family's descendants as chief men dwelling in Jerusalem. God is often kinder to a family than its head has been.

pos: n. (father of Shammah, one of David's three mighty men; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Age', commonly explained as a fugitive, from a root meaning to flee; named once, 2 Samuel 23:11.
biblical_def: Agee is named once, as the father of one of the three: “And after him was Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. And the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people fled from the Philistines” (2 Samuel 23:11). The detail is almost comic in its smallness — a field of lentils — and what his son did in it is the point: “But he stood in the midst of the ground, and defended it, and slew the Philistines: and the LORD wrought a great victory” (2 Samuel 23:12). The same formula closes the account of the man before him: “He arose, and smote the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clave unto the sword: and the LORD wrought a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to spoil” (2 Samuel 23:10). Twice in two verses the chapter says who won: the LORD wrought a great victory. And the whole roll is counted at the end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). Agee's name may mean fugitive, and his son is remembered for refusing to run.

corruption_summary: The exploits of the three are read as hero-worship, where the chapter twice attributes the victory to the LORD and reserves to the men only their standing fast.
corruption_paragraphs: A chapter of warrior anecdotes invites the charge of hero-worship, and the deeds are indeed extraordinary. But the writer has taken care to say where the credit lies. Of Eleazar's stand and of Shammah's the same sentence is used — the LORD wrought a great victory — and in Eleazar's case the people who had fled are said to have returned only to take spoil. The men are credited with not running; God is credited with the outcome. That is the exact proportion Scripture keeps everywhere between human faithfulness and divine power.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of a small field. Shammah did not defend a city or a king; he defended a patch of lentils that everyone else judged not worth dying for, and the Holy Ghost wrote it down and called the result a great victory of the LORD. Faithfulness in a thing that looks trivial is not trivial.

pos: n. (a son of Coz in the genealogies of Judah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Anub, commonly explained as bound together, or confederate; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:8.
biblical_def: Anub occurs once, in the same verse that gives Aharhel: “And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum” (1 Chronicles 4:8). The chapter is the great Judahite register, opening with the tribe's heads: “The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1). Two verses after Anub's, the list is interrupted by the one thing in the chapter that everybody knows: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Then it resumes with trades and towns: “The sons of Shelah the son of Judah were, Er the father of Lecah, and Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21). Anub is a name in that company — linen-weavers, potters, a man who prayed and was heard, and households whose only remaining history is that God kept their names.

corruption_summary: Ordinary work is treated as separate from the service of God, where Scripture names households by their trades inside the register of the covenant tribe.
corruption_paragraphs: A division our age takes for granted — sacred work on one side, ordinary labour on the other — does not survive this chapter. The Chronicler lists in one breath the fathers of towns, the house of them that wrought fine linen, the potters, a man who prayed and was answered, and the families of men we know nothing else about. All of it is the register of the tribe through which Christ came. Scripture knows a distinction between the ministry and other callings, and it does not know a distinction between holy work and honest work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's record of a people includes its weavers. Whatever is done in faith and to His glory is counted, and the tribe of Judah appears in Scripture not as a line of kings only but as households with crafts, towns, prayers and names — Anub among them.
